newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tens of thousands in Hong Kong mourn Tiananmen.
newsitem.headline: Tens of thousands in Hong Kong mourn Tiananmen.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Hong Kong people staged a poignant memorial on Wednesday to pro-democracy demonstrators in China who perished in 1989 at the hands of a government that will take over the British colony very soon.
Many shed a tear as they sang along to anthems associated with the annual candle-lit vigils held yearly since 1989 in a park named after Britain's 19th century Queen Victoria.
A towering grey "Pillar of Shame" statue of twisted human bodies depicting oppression stood spotlit in the dark.

The singing swelled as the grandfather of Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement, Szeto Wah, dubbed a subversive by Beijing, lit a torch and vowed that the spirit of June 4 would live on beyond Hong Kong's handover to China at midnight on June 30.
Scuffles broke out in the early hours of Thursday morning when police blocked students from transporting the Pillar of Shame onto a campus in defiance of university authorities.
Hong Kong Student leader Wong Chun-sing said they wanted to display the monument outside the University of Hong Kong student union but had been refused permission.
They took the statue to the campus anyway but police and university security guards refused to let them in for several hours before relenting in order to clear the highway.
There were no reports of arrests or injury.
Wednesday's demonstrators urged Beijing to withdraw its verdict that the student-led protesters cut down by Chinese troops in Tiananmen Square eight years ago were counter-revolutionaries.

But there were few signs of the anger and disgust which propelled one million people onto the streets of Hong Kong eight years ago in horror over the ruthlessness of the Chinese leadership in suppressing the protests.
Also gone were the crude effigies of Chinese leaders, the defaced Chinese communist flags and explicit banners calling for the overthrow of the "Butchers of Beijing" brandished in 1989.

The Tiananmen Square crackdown was a watershed in Hong Kong's drawn out 13-year transition from British colony to a quasi-autonomous part of China, sparking the birth of a pro-democracy movement and smashing the myth that Hong Kong people were staunchly apolitical.
But, in stark contrast to the post-1989 gloom, Hong Kong's 6.4 million people now view their future after the handover with a considerable degree of equanimity, opinion polls show.

Many are banking on Beijing honouring its promise, made in the 1984 Sino-British treaty governing the handover, to permit fiercely individualistic Hong Kong people to retain intact their freedoms and capitalist way of life.
The 55,000 people who gathered this year in Victoria Park gave few indications that they fear retribution from across the border after the British depart.
The sight of People's Liberation Army (PLA) tanks crushing unarmed student protesters in 1989 horrified Hong Kong.
Yet the community took in stride the low-key arrival in April of an advance PLA guard, unarmed in accordance with Britain's wishes, to prepare facilities for a future Chinese garrison.

The Hong Kong economy is powering ahead, the stock market is booming and the tide has turned on a middle class exodus of up to half a million people after the Tiananmen massacre. Many are returning with the assurance of a foreign passport tucked away.

Only a dozen or so Chinese dissidents who escaped to Hong Kong, many of them in the wake of Tiananmen, remain in the British colony and are expected to get asylum overseas before the handover, said activists and legislator Lau Chin-shek.

"Many left this year. Nineteen left last week," Lau said. "We are very confident those eligible for political refugee status will be able to leave. Even the Hong Kong government wants them to leave...It is helping them."
Hong Kong's homegrown democracy activists face the political wilderness because China will dissolve the elected legislature when it takes over on July 1, but they appear uncowed.

Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's democracy party, vowed he would mark the June 4 anniversary next year even if, as many fear, such a demonstration is banned by the incoming administration led by former shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa.

Lee has campaigned overseas against China's plans, endorsed by Tung, to appoint a provisional legislature in place of the elected chamber and dilute civil liberties, including curbs of demonstrations in the name of social stability.

"Mr Tung should have come here tonight to see how peaceful the people are," Lee told reporters. "I'm happy about Hong Kong being returned to China but why can we not retain all our existing freedoms?"
